The Bahá’í writings portray justice as foundational to human society. In *God Passes By*, Shoghi Effendi describes it as ["the light of men" and their "guardian"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) — *God Passes By*, upon which ["the organization of the world and the tranquillity of mankind"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) depend. Its "two pillars" are identified as ["reward and punishment"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) — *God Passes By*.

Beyond these cosmic and societal dimensions, the writings also offer a personal measure for moral action. Howard Colby Ives notes Bahá’u’lláh's definition: ["Wert thou to observe justice choose for others that which thou choosest for thyself"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/howard-colby-ingles_portals-to-freedom#p538) — *Portals to Freedom*. Furthermore, as recorded in *The Hidden Words*, Bahá’u’lláh states that ["Justice is to be loved above all"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/earl-redman_abdul-baha-in-their-midst#p116) — *Abdu'l-Bahá in Their Midst*.

Dear friend,

It is a true joy to look into this with you. The Bahá’í writings speak of justice not merely as a rule for settling disputes, but as a living, radiant power at the very heart of human existence. 

Shoghi Effendi writes in *God Passes By* that justice is extolled as ["the light of men"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) and ["their guardian"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510), as well as ["the revealer of the secrets of the world of being, and the standard-bearer of love and bounty"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) — affirming that upon it depends ["the organization of the world and the tranquillity of mankind"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510). He further characterizes its ["two pillars"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) as ["_reward_ _and_ _punishment_"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) and ["the sources of life"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_510) to the human race (*God Passes By*). 

There is a wonderful discovery in the texts regarding how we are to measure justice in our own daily lives. Howard Colby Ives, recalling the teachings in *Portals to Freedom*, points us directly to Bahá’u’lláh's own standard:

> "Wert thou to observe justice choose for others that
which thou choosest for thyself," [^2] how many of us would

*(Portals to Freedom)*

This turning away from our own narrow personal reactions toward choosing for others what we would choose for ourselves strikes right at the flaccidity of moral fibre. 

When we look deeper into the source of this virtue, J. Ruh-Angiz Bolles records in *Shoghi Effendi on Laws, Administration, and Prophecy* a passage from *Gleanings* stating, ["Know verily that the essence of Justice and the source thereof are both embodied in the ordinances prescribed by Him...Were His law to be such as to strike terror into the hearts of all that are in heaven and on earth that law is naught but manifest justice..."](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/j-ruh-angiz-bolles_shoghi-effendi-on-laws-administration-and-prophecy#p6). Earl Redman's *Abdu'l-Bahá in Their Midst* reminds us simply of the declaration found in the *Hidden Words* that ["Justice is to be loved above all."](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/ear

That is a very natural doubt to have, especially when human laws and institutions so often reflect the will of whoever holds power. 

Religious traditions, however, generally place the standard of justice entirely outside human hands. In the Qur'án, justice belongs to a divine standard, asking, ["Is not God a most just of judges?"](https://oceanlibrary.com/quran_palmer-tr?paraId=para_3792) — *The Qur’ân (Palmer)*. Similarly, in the Gathas, the bounteous spirit chooses ["the (Divine) Righteousness"](https://oceanlibrary.com/gathas_zoroaster?paraId=para_50) — *The Gathas* as an objective reality rather than a political decree. Even when human authorities exercise power unequally—as the Buddhist collection illustrates, noting how a ["goat butcher is empowered to beat or bind or slay or treat as he likes"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-l?paraId=para_1064) — *Sutra Collection (L)* a poor person for a crime they might treat differently in someone else—the spiritual texts themselves typically appeal to a higher, unchanging measure against which earthly power is judged. 

How do you feel these texts distinguish true justice from human power?

That view makes complete sense. When we see laws enforced by police and courts holding communities together day to day, it is easy to conclude that force and legislation are what truly maintain order. 

Yet the sources suggest the reverse causation. In *The World Order of Bahá’u’lláh*, Shoghi Effendi quotes Bahá’u’lláh describing ["Religion... is the greatest of all means for the establishment of order in the world"](https://oceanlibrary.com/world-order-of-bahaullah_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_467) — *The World Order of Bahá’u’lláh*. From this perspective, religion shapes the inner conscience, making external force largely unnecessary. 

Similarly, Lao-tzu argues in the *Tao Te Ching* that ["the more display there is of legislation, the more thieves and robbers there are"](https://oceanlibrary.com/tao-te-ching_lao-tzu?paraId=para_279) — *Tao Te Ching*. The materialist view sees religion as a tool of the state, but these traditions suggest that laws multiply only when inner, moral order begins to fail.

It is entirely natural to look at the disorder around us and wish a government could simply step in and close the door on wrongdoing. 

Yet ‘Abdu’l-Bahá suggests that relying on punishment—["the body politic is engaged day and night in devising penal laws"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha?paraId=para_952) and building prisons—actually brings about ["the degradation of morals and the subversion of character"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha?paraId=para_952) rather than true reform (*Some Answered Questions*). From this view, lasting order grows from within, when a society bends its efforts toward education and ["praiseworthy virtues"](https://oceanlibrary.com/some-answered-questions_abdul-baha?paraId=para_952) (*Some Answered Questions*). Confucius similarly envisions a state where goodness so thoroughly guides the people that a country could ["do away with capital punishments"](https://oceanlibrary.com/analects_confucius?paraId=para_553) altogether (*The Analects*). 

When compliance is forced, the inner struggle that builds moral strength is bypassed. What do you think leaves a deeper mark on a person: choosing the right path freely, or having the choice removed?

That feeling is something people have wrestled with across traditions for ages. Confucius himself listed among his heaviest burdens ["failure to improve in the virtues"](https://oceanlibrary.com/analects_confucius?paraId=para_247) and ["inability to walk according to knowledge received as to what is right and just"](https://oceanlibrary.com/analects_confucius?paraId=para_247) (*The Analects*). 

The point of trying is not about achieving perfection on the first try, but the continued turning back toward what is true and good. As Vyasa tells his son in *The Mahabharata*, the work is to ["practise righteousness"](https://oceanlibrary.com/mahabharata-12_vyasa?paraId=para_1768) and remain ["firmly devoted to righteousness"](https://oceanlibrary.com/mahabharata-12_vyasa?paraId=para_1768) despite the difficulty of the effort (*The Mahabharata 12*). The struggle itself matters.

You are noticing a real parallel in how both traditions describe the Divine entering the world through distinct figures. 

The Bahá'í writings speak of the teachers who appear across history as ["Manifestations that are essentially one and the same"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah?paraId=para_204) — ["expressions of one Truth"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah?paraId=para_204) despite their differing missions, while Hindu texts describe avatāras as ["portions of the same Supreme Being"](https://oceanlibrary.com/mahabharata-6_vyasa?paraId=fn_57). 

Yet there is a subtle distinction in the sources regarding *what* is descending. Bahá'u’lláh emphasizes that the differences in their words arise from ["this difference in their station and mission"](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah?paraId=para_204) rather than a difference in the underlying Truth itself. 

You might enjoy reading further in [*The Kitáb-i-Íqán*](https://oceanlibrary.com/kitab-i-iqan_bahaullah?paraId=para_204) to see how Bahá'u'lláh describes the shared station of the prophets, or looking at *The Bhagavad-Gita* to explore how avatāras manifest. Which of those traditions would you like to step into next?

That is a very common thought, but the writings of the Bahá’í Faith see it differently. Shoghi Effendi writes that the faith has [*“assimilated, by virtue of its creative, its regulative and ennobling energies, the varied races, nationalities, creeds and classes”*](https://oceanlibrary.com/world-order-of-bahaullah_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_498) — *The World Order of Bahá’u’lláh*. 

Rather than viewing all religions as identical, the texts suggest that different creeds and peoples find a common home under its shadow while preserving their distinct loyalties. It is less about every tradition being the same, and more about a unifying energy that transforms outlooks and brings diverse streams together as [*“lovers of mankind”*](https://oceanlibrary.com/world-order-of-bahaullah_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_498) — *The World Order of Bahá’u’lláh*. 

There is a wonderful depth to explore here about how distinct traditions can be deeply respected without erasing their unique voices. What part of that relationship between different faiths interests you most?

You are entirely right to look closely at what Bahá'u'lláh Himself wrote, as many of His teachings on this subject are recorded through the explanations of 'Abdu'l-Bahá and later writers rather than direct quotes widely known in His own primary texts. 

Yet the sources record that this principle is rooted directly in His revelation. Mírzá Aḥmad Sohrab notes that ["In the revelation of Bahá’u’lláh, men and women stand shoulder to shoulder"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/mirza-ahmad-sohrab_abdul-baha-in-egypt#p1168) — *'Abdu''l-Bahá in Egypt*, and that ["For His Holiness Bahá’u’lláh hath willed it so"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/mirza-ahmad-sohrab_abdul-baha-in-egypt#p1168) — *'Abdu''l-Bahá in Egypt*. David Hofman similarly lists ["the equality of the sexes"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/david-hofman_george-townshend-hand-of-the-cause-of-god#p1048) among ["the humanitarian principles which are explicit in His teaching"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/david-hofman_george-townshend-hand-of-the-cause-of-god#p1048) — *George Townshend, Hand of the Cause of God*. 

Would you like to explore how 'Abdu'l-Bahá expanded upon these specific writings during His travels in the West?

That is a wonderful feeling to carry. Gladys Weeden writes in her pilgrim notes of how she came to see that ["we are a world family dedicated to the unity of mankind"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/gladys-weeden-pilgrim-notes#p528) — *Gladys Weeden Pilgrim Notes*. 

There is a small, lovely detail she shares from her time learning about this community that I think you might enjoy as well. She notes that ["in the word 'unity' the 'you' comes before the 'I.'"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/gladys-weeden-pilgrim-notes#p528) — *Gladys Weeden Pilgrim Notes*. 

It is a simple reminder of how turning toward others is woven right into the very word we use for togetherness.

You are entirely right to connect the two, as they are both major works by the same author, Bahá’u’lláh. But they are distinct books written at different times. 

Shoghi Effendi explains that the *Kitáb-i-Aqdas* was promulgated as a later development, noting that it was ["Alluded to in the Kitáb-i-Íqán"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_499) — *God Passes By*. 

So while the *Íqán* came first and points toward what follows, the *Aqdas* is specifically known as the ["Most Holy Book"](https://oceanlibrary.com/god-passes-by_shoghi-effendi?paraId=para_499) — *God Passes By*, serving as the principal repository of Bahá’í law.

I am so sorry for the loss of your father. 

Different writings describe different paths for the soul. In Hindu tradition, *The Bhagavad-Gita* describes how the departing soul's inner state shapes its movement, noting that ["it goeth to the place"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bhagavad-gita?paraId=para_204) of truth if fixed in soothfastness, while a soul dying in ignorance ["is born anew in some unlighted womb"](https://oceanlibrary.com/bhagavad-gita?paraId=para_204) — *The Bhagavad-Gita*. In Buddhist texts, followers also ask about ["What are his movements after death?"](https://oceanlibrary.com/oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-a-part-1?paraId=para_362) regarding those who have passed away — *Sutra Collection (A, Part-1)*.

That is a question people have asked across traditions. In Bahá'í accounts, when a pilgrim asked why prayer is necessary ["since presumably God knows the wishes of all hearts"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/ethel-stephana_abbas-effendi-his-personality-work-and-followers#p35), the reply pointed away from informing God and toward the soul's own growth. 

While the sources record that ["Every single thing is before His sight"](https://oceanlibrary.com/holy-quran_yusuf-tr?paraId=para_1950) (*The Holy Qur-an (Yusuf Ali)*), the Bahá'í pilgrim notes emphasize individual responsibility: ["Every man is his own priest, is responsible for his own soul growth"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/ethel-stephana_abbas-effendi-his-personality-work-and-followers#p35) (*Abbas Effendi: His personality, work, and followers*). Even when prayer books are provided by Bahá'u'lláh to ["fit the needs which may arise"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/ethel-stephana_abbas-effendi-his-personality-work-and-followers#p35), using them is left completely to the individual. 

So prayer isn't given to inform the Knower, but perhaps to change the one who asks. What part of that connection between prayer and soul growth catches your interest?

It is completely natural for a Christian to feel cautious about how another tradition views Christ. 

The records of the Bahá'í tradition state that Bahá'u'lláh ["praised and sanctified all the Divine Holy Manifestations, and offered His Holiness Christ such a praise, beyond the description and imagination"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/frances-orr-allen_abdul-bahas-visit-to-california#p2657) — *Abdu'l-Bahá's Visit to California*. Moreover, the sources note that ["Bahá’u’lláh wrote many commentaries on the Gospel, bringing to light its inner significances"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/frances-orr-allen_abdul-bahas-visit-to-california#p2657) — *Abdu'l-Bahá's Visit to California*. 

Whether that honour matches Christian understandings is a different question, but the texts themselves record a deep reverence. I hope that offers a helpful window into what the literature actually says.

The passages provided here do not contain any mention of Jesus. 

While the library record includes works on Islamic tradition and commentary—such as *The Qur’ân* ([1](https://oceanlibrary.com/quran_palmer-tr?paraId=para_146)), Ṣaḥíḥ al-Bukhárí ([2](https://oceanlibrary.com/sahih-al-bukhari?paraId=para_13153)), Ibn Rushd's *The Philosophy and Theology* ([3](https://oceanlibrary.com/philosophy-and-theology_ibn-rushd?paraId=para_141)), Majlisi's *Hayat Al-Qulub* ([4](https://oceanlibrary.com/hayat-al-qulub-vol-1_muhammad-majlisi?paraId=para_425)), Todd Lawson's study of the Báb's commentary ([5](https://oceanlibrary.com/quran-commentary-of-sayyid-muhammad-the-bab_todd-lawson?paraId=para_1373)), and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim ([6](https://oceanlibrary.com/sahih-muslim-book-7_muslim-ibn-al-hajjaj?paraId=para_193))—none of these specific excerpts touch on what the Qur'án says about Jesus. 

If you would like to explore this question, you might try asking from a wider selection of texts that include verses addressing Jesus (known as *‘Īsā* in the Qur'án), where he is spoken of as a messenger, the word of God, and a sign to mankind.

I cannot answer how Buddhism describes compassion from the provided texts, as the passages in our library touch on dependent co-arising, the discipline of monks, sensory restraint, and the doctrine of karma, but they do not mention compassion. 

What the library does show very clearly in these texts is the close attention given to mental restraint and action—such as how a monk "does not grasp at any theme or details" (*Digha Nikaya 11 - Kevaddha Sutta*), protecting the senses from unskillful qualities like greed and distress. 

If you would like to explore this further, perhaps you might ask about how these teachings on mental restraint or karma shape Buddhist ethics, or we might look into other texts that address the heart's response to suffering. What feels like the right next step for your reading?

Yes, a scientist can truly believe. The sources show that many find no fundamental opposition between empirical inquiry and faith. In the Bahá'í tradition, Doris McKay records the teaching that ["Science and religion will enhance and prove each other"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/doris-mckay_memories-of-bahais#p34) — asking, ["How can one truth contradict another truth?"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/pilgrim-notes/doris-mckay_memories-of-bahais#p34) — *Memories of Bahá’ís*. 

Similarly, Buddhist commentary suggests that ["A scientific world such as todays will be able to accept gladly all ten tenets of the Kalama Sutta"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-hijk?paraId=para_1080) because ["There is not the least contradiction between the principles of science and those of the Kalama Sutta"](https://oceanlibrary.com/sutra-collection-hijk?paraId=para_1080) — *Sutra Collection (HIJK)*. 

At the same time, traditions like Judaism and Islam direct inquiry toward the Creator behind the natural order, as when the Psalms declare, ["Know ye that the LORD he is God: it is he that hath made us, and not we ourselves"](https://oceanlibrary.com/book-of-psalms-tehilim_david?paraId=para_1778) — *Psalms*. The evidence suggests that for many, the rigor of science and the conviction of belief walk side by side.

The provided writings do not mention quantum computing. 

However, Adib Taherzadeh records in [*The Revelation of Bahá’u’lláh vol. 3*](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/adib-taherzadeh_the-revelation-of-bahaullah-vol-3#p1935) that Bahá’u’lláh affirmed He would ["raise up scientists of great calibre who will bring about such marvellous technological achievements"](https://siftersearch.com/library/bahai/bahai-books/adib-taherzadeh_the-revelation-of-bahaullah-vol-3#p1935) that people could not yet imagine them.
